paper_title: XTRA: Unifying Cache Coherence and Concurrency Control for Distributed Transactions in a CXL Pod [SOSP 2026]
readme:
# XTRA

XTRA is the research prototype for **“XTRA: Unifying Cache Coherence and
Concurrency Control for Distributed Transactions in a CXL Pod,”** accepted to
ACM SOSP 2026.

XTRA is built on the [Tigon](https://github.com/ut-datasys/tigon) (OSDI 2025)
codebase. This repository retains Tigon's VM-based CXL-pod infrastructure,
benchmark framework, and the Tigon and Sundial-CXL baselines used in our
evaluation. Sharing the infrastructure keeps the VM topology, workloads, CXL
transport, and runtime environment consistent across all systems.

The repository contains:

- XTRA (`protocol/XTRA/`);
- Tigon (`protocol/TwoPLPasha/`);
- Sundial-CXL (`protocol/SundialPasha/`);
- YCSB, SmallBank, and TPC-C benchmark drivers;
- scripts for creating a VM-based CXL pod and running experiments.

In this artifact, the Tigon and Sundial-CXL baselines are based on the
implementations released with the original Tigon artifact and retain their
original runtime identifiers, `TwoPLPasha` and `SundialPasha`, respectively.

## Emulating a CXL Pod with VMs

We emulate an eight-host CXL pod with eight VMs on one physical machine. Each
VM represents one host and has private local memory, while all VMs access the
same 128 GiB region through `ivshmem`. The shared region is backed either by a
real CXL memory NUMA node or by a remote NUMA node.

![VM-based CXL pod emulation](emulation.png)

*Figure reproduced from the [Tigon artifact](https://github.com/ut-datasys/tigon).*

The evaluation uses 8 VMs, 4 vCPUs per VM, 28 GiB of local memory per VM, and
3 transaction workers per VM. The original Tigon artifact uses five
vCPUs per VM: three for transaction workers, one for message dispatch, and one
for group-commit logging. Since all systems in our evaluation use per-worker
CXL-backed WAL, no dedicated logging thread is needed, allowing the baselines to
retain three transaction workers on our four-vCPU VMs. The baselines reserve one
vCPU for migration-message passing. XTRA does not require migration messages,
but we keep the same three-worker configuration and do not use the remaining
vCPU for transaction execution.

## Important Notes

- Run all commands from the repository root.
- The VM scripts change host-level CPU settings and should be run on a dedicated
  test machine.
- Reconfiguring a DAX device as system RAM destroys data stored on that device.
- Motor requires a separate multi-machine RDMA testbed. We provide the Figure 8
  and 9 reference results measured on our RDMA cluster in
  [`results/motor`](results/motor). Refer to the
  [Motor artifact](https://github.com/minghust/motor) to rerun that baseline.

## Testbed Setup

### Hardware Requirements

#### Option A

- A machine with at least 32 CPU cores on one socket;
- A CXL memory device with at least 128 GB capacity, connected to that socket;
- Ubuntu 22.04.

#### Option B (if CXL memory is not available)

- A two-socket machine with at least 32 CPU cores per socket;
- At least 128 GB of memory on the remote NUMA node to emulate CXL memory;
- Ubuntu 22.04.

The provided configuration allocates 28,672 MiB (28 GiB) of local memory to
each VM. Eight guests therefore require 224 GiB on the compute NUMA node, plus
additional capacity for host and QEMU overhead.

### Setup VM-based CXL Pod Emulation from Scratch

1. Clone the repository.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/cszjyang/xtra.git
cd xtra
```

2. Set up the host.

```bash
./scripts/setup.sh HOST
```

3. Build VM image.

```bash
./emulation/image/make_vm_img.sh
```

4. Launch eight 4-vCPU VMs.

For Option A, first expose the CXL device as a CPU-less system-RAM NUMA node.
Replace `dax0.0` and the last argument (`2`) with the device and CXL NUMA node
on your machine.

```bash
sudo daxctl reconfigure-device --mode=system-ram dax0.0 --force
sudo ./emulation/start_vms.sh --using-old-img --cxl 0 4 8 0 2
```

For Option B, replace the last argument (`1`) with the remote NUMA node used to
back the shared region.

```bash
sudo ./emulation/start_vms.sh --using-old-img --cxl 0 4 8 1 1
```

5. Set up the VMs.

```bash
./scripts/setup.sh VMS 8
```

## Build and Deploy

The build uses C++17, Clang/Clang++ 15, LLD 15, jemalloc, Folly, and the bundled
`dependencies/cxlalloc/libcxlalloc_static.a`.

Build and deploy both XTRA configurations to all eight VMs:

```bash
./scripts/run.sh COMPILE_SYNC 8
```

The command creates two independent compile-time configurations and deploys all
six benchmark executables:

- `build/hcc` uses `ENABLE_LAMPORT_FAST=OFF` and produces `bench_ycsb`,
  `bench_smallbank`, and `bench_tpcc`;
- `build/nhcc` uses `ENABLE_LAMPORT_FAST=ON` and produces the corresponding
  `_nhcc` executables, such as `bench_ycsb_nhcc`.

`XTRA` denotes the default HCC configuration; `XTRA-NHCC` enables LamportFast
for non-cache-coherent CXL memory. Experiment scripts pass the selected system
name to `run.sh`, which chooses the appropriate executable. All baselines use
the unsuffixed HCC executables. No rebuild or redeployment is required when
switching between `XTRA` and `XTRA-NHCC` experiments.

## Kick-the-Tires Example

The default configuration in `scripts/run_ycsb.py` runs XTRA on the small YCSB
configuration: 2.4 million records in total, 3 transaction workers per VM,
10 accesses per transaction, 5% writes, and Zipf `theta=0.7`.

```bash
python3 scripts/run_ycsb.py results/kick-the-tires
```

The raw benchmark log contains an aggregate result line in the following form
(abbreviated; numbers may differ):

```text
Global Stats: total_commit: 1.91638e+06 ... P50_latency: 11 us P99_latency: 16.0416 us
```

`total_commit` is the aggregate throughput across all participating hosts, in
transactions/s, while `P50_latency` and `P99_latency` are measured in
microseconds. The script preserves the complete log, extracts these metrics
into `summary.csv`, and records the experiment configuration and source
revision in `manifest.json`. All files are written under
`results/kick-the-tires/ycsb/`. Use a fresh result root when running the script
again.

The 40-second run includes a 10-second warmup followed by the 30-second
measurement interval used in the paper. It typically completes in about
5 minutes on the authors' setup. Do not run it concurrently with another
experiment on the same VMs.

## Experimental Configuration

### Evaluated Default Configuration

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Hosts | 8 VMs |
| Resources per VM | 4 vCPUs and 28 GiB local memory |
| Transaction workers | 3 per VM |
| Shared CXL memory | 128 GiB |
| Coordination Directory / HCC budget | 200 MiB |
| CXL transport | Enabled (`USE_CXL_TRANS=1`) |
| Output thread | Disabled (`USE_OUTPUT_THREAD=0`) |
| Logging | CXL-backed WAL |
| Warmup / measurement | 10 seconds / 30 seconds |

Tigon, Sundial-CXL, and XTRA use the same VM resources, worker count, CXL
capacity, workload inputs, and measurement interval. The baselines retain their
original logging control flow, while the storage backend is replaced with the
same CXL-backed WAL used by XTRA.

### Workload Scales

The sizes below are totals across all eight VMs. `KEYS` is the per-VM value
passed to YCSB and SmallBank; `PARTITION_NUM_PER_HOST` is the per-VM TPC-C
warehouse count.

| Workload | Small | Medium | Large | Main settings |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| YCSB | 2.4M records (`KEYS=300000`) | 10M (`KEYS=1250000`) | 40M (`KEYS=5000000`) | 4-byte keys, 128-byte values, 10 accesses/transaction, 5% writes, Zipf `theta=0.7` |
| SmallBank | 1.2M accounts (`KEYS=150000`) | 5M (`KEYS=625000`) | 20M (`KEYS=2500000`) | Standard transaction mix, Zipf `theta=0.7` |
| TPC-C | 24 warehouses (`PARTITION_NUM_PER_HOST=3`) | 240 (`=30`) | 960 (`=120`) | Standard mix; approximately 60%/90% cross-warehouse NewOrder/Payment transactions |

For YCSB, `RW_RATIO` is the read percentage, so 5% writes corresponds to
`RW_RATIO=95`. The paper uses a global key space, configured with
`GLOBAL_KEY_SPACE=true` and `CROSS_RATIO=0`.

### Figure Reproduction Scripts

The AE scripts expose one paper figure and workload per file. All experiment
parameters are fixed in the corresponding script; the only required argument is
the result root directory. Approximate wall times shown below were observed on
the authors' eight-VM setup and may vary by machine:

```bash
python3 scripts/fig8_ycsb.py results/paper-run       # About 1 hour
python3 scripts/fig8_smallbank.py results/paper-run  # About 1 hour
python3 scripts/fig8_tpcc.py results/paper-run       # About 1 hour

python3 scripts/fig9_ycsb.py results/paper-run       # About 1.5 hours
python3 scripts/fig9_smallbank.py results/paper-run  # About 1.5 hours
python3 scripts/fig9_tpcc.py results/paper-run       # About 1 hour

python3 scripts/fig10_ycsb.py results/paper-run       # About 1.5 hours
python3 scripts/fig10_smallbank.py results/paper-run  # About 1.5 hours
python3 scripts/fig10_tpcc.py results/paper-run       # About 2 hours

python3 scripts/fig11_ycsb.py results/paper-run       # About 1 hour
python3 scripts/fig11_smallbank.py results/paper-run  # About 1 hour
python3 scripts/fig11_tpcc.py results/paper-run       # About 1 hour
```

Figure 12 requires additional build variants for its coherence comparison and
is provided on the `figure12-workflow` branch:

```bash
git fetch origin
git switch figure12-workflow
./scripts/run.sh COMPILE_FIG12_SYNC 8

# Run the following Figure 12 reproduction scripts from the figure12-workflow branch.
python3 scripts/fig12_ycsb.py results/paper-run       # About 20 minutes
python3 scripts/fig12_smallbank.py results/paper-run  # About 20 minutes
python3 scripts/fig12_tpcc.py results/paper-run       # About 20 minutes

# Restore the main branch and standard executables after the Figure 12 experiments.
git switch main
./scripts/run.sh COMPILE_SYNC 8
```

For one complete reproduction of Figures 8--12, use a new result root; all
commands above may share it. With `results/paper-run`, for example, Figure 8
YCSB results are written under `results/paper-run/fig8/ycsb/`.

Each Figure/workload directory contains per-configuration raw logs,
`manifest.json`, and an aggregated `summary.csv`. The manifest records the
configuration matrices and source revision. The summary contains one row per
successfully completed benchmark configuration, including its system,
Figure-specific dimensions, and the throughput and P50/P99 latency extracted
from its `Global Stats` line. The summaries for Figures 8 and 9 also include the
Motor reference rows from [`results/motor`](results/motor). If a configuration
fails, the script stops and retains `.partial` files; existing results are not
overwritten.

### Configurable Workload Scripts

The `fig*.py` scripts above use the fixed configurations from the paper. For a
custom experiment matrix, edit the list-valued `configs` dictionary in one of
the following workload scripts:

```bash
python3 scripts/run_ycsb.py results/custom-run
python3 scripts/run_smallbank.py results/custom-run
python3 scripts/run_tpcc.py results/custom-run
```

Each script runs every combination in its `configs` dictionary and writes the
results under the corresponding `ycsb/`, `smallbank/`, or `tpcc/` subdirectory.
The three workloads may share one fresh result root; rerunning the same workload
requires another result root.

The lower-level execution interface builds on Tigon's `run.sh`; inherited
parameters retain the meanings documented in the
[Tigon artifact](https://github.com/ut-datasys/tigon#test-tigon-in-various-configurations).
The workload scripts expose the evaluated customization interface, with
XTRA-specific additions and constraints documented next to their `configs`
entries. Shared execution modes are fixed for the validated workflow and
documented in [`scripts/common.py`](scripts/common.py). Use the Python workload
scripts rather than the positional `scripts/run.sh` interface for custom
experiments.
